evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (Chinese characters database, CUHK)
evidence.text: The database analyzes the bronze form as 巾 semantic plus 尚 phonetic, with the original sense ‘lower-body clothing’. It reports the graph used in that sense in the Zifan bell inscription, “衣、常(裳)、帶、巿,” and Warring States bamboo texts including 新蔡楚簡 and 睡虎地秦簡. It reports a bronze use for 常 meaning ‘custom/rule’ in 陳侯因敦, and says ancient texts also sometimes mix 常 and 嘗, with that confusion declining gradually after the Ming and Qing. These are database assertions; the inspected page did not supply inscription dates or images.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 說文釋形; 字樣說明; 釋義
evidence.text: The entry quotes Shuowen’s analysis 下帬也。从巾，尚聲 and its variant 常或从衣. It says the clothing sense later came to be written 裳 and 常 became dedicated to ‘frequently’. The entry separately documents senses ‘rules/ethical order’, ‘ordinary’, ‘lasting’, ‘regular’, and ‘frequently’, with literary examples, including citations to the Book of Documents, Hou Hanshu, Zuo Zhuan, Laozi, Zhuangzi, and Xunzi. The entry provides no date of first use for each sense; its classical citations establish textual attestations, not necessarily the date of composition or the graph’s first occurrence.
evidence.title: 常 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, text of 說文解字 and 段玉裁注
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry says ‘lower skirt/garment; from 巾, 尚 phonetic’ and records 裳 as an alternative written with 衣. Duan Yucai’s Qing commentary cites 釋名 on 衣/裳 and says 裳 became the current graph while 常 fell out of use for the garment sense; he further states that 巾 was chosen for the squared fabric and that the character extended to the ‘constant’ sense. This is a historical lexicographic account, not independent proof of the graph’s earliest formation.
evidence.kind: primary historical dictionary text with later commentary
evidence.title: 說文解字「常」

evidence.text: The record lists Chu-script manuscript forms, small seal script, and Shuowen, and describes the lower 巾 as semantic and 尚 as phonetic. The inspected text did not expose image contents, so no visual comparison or detailed graphic change is claimed here.

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 常 entry (historical phonology tables citing named systems)
evidence.text: The entry gives Mandarin cháng and Cantonese soeng4. Its table gives Middle Chinese Baxter transcription dzyang and Guangyun fanqie 市羊切; it lists Old Chinese Baxter–Sagart system 1.1 /*[d]aŋ/ and Zhengzhang Shangfang 2003 /*djaŋ/. The separate 尚 entry gives Mandarin shàng, Middle Chinese dzyangH for the departing-tone reading, and Zhengzhang /*djaŋs/ for that reading; it also records a level-tone historical reading with Middle Chinese dzyang and Zhengzhang /*djaŋ/. Thus the cited Zhengzhang forms support a close sound relationship for 常 and the level-tone 尚 reading, while the alternate departing-tone 尚 reading has a final -s. These are reconstructions, not directly recorded ancient pronunciations.
evidence.title: 常 - Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, 尚 entry (historical phonology tables citing named systems)
evidence.text: For 尚 the entry gives Mandarin shàng and an additional level-tone historical reading. In Zhengzhang Shangfang 2003 it lists /*djaŋ/ for the level-tone reading and /*djaŋs/ for the departing-tone reading. Its Middle Chinese table gives dzyang for the level-tone reading and dzyangH for the departing-tone reading. This supports the phonetic comparison with 常 at the level-tone reading; it does not establish the pronunciation or name of any depicted object, and no whole-graph loan from 尚 is required by the phonetic-component analysis.
evidence.title: 尚 - Wiktionary

evidence.text: The database analyzes bronze 常 as 巾 semantic plus 尚 phonetic, with a lower-body garment sense. It reports that 常 and 裳 were originally graphic variants for this sense; later 常 was used for frequent/regular meanings and 裳 retained the garment sense. Examples it names include the Zifan bell inscription and Warring States bamboo slips for clothing, and a bronze inscription for ‘custom/law’. It also reports historical mixing of 常 and 嘗. These are database reports; the inspected entry gives no artifact dates.

gaps: No accessible source in this search established a Shang oracle-bone form for 常. The inspected paleographic database lists Chu manuscripts, small seal, and Shuowen; its page text did not expose glyph images.

The claim that 尚’s own graphic origin depicts a raised platform is an interpretation reported by the CUHK database, with named scholarly attribution; its alternative element history is not independently evaluated here. This uncertainty does not undermine 尚’s later phonetic role in 常.

The database attributes the clothing sense to bronze and Warring States examples, but exact object dates, earliest occurrence, and manuscript/inscription images were not verified. The Shuowen record and later citations are not a substitute for dating the earliest attestation.

A competing account reported by CUHK, attributing to 朱駿聲 the view that 常 originally meant a flag and 裳 denoted the garment, is judged doubtful there based on bronze uses. This remains a documented disagreement; no primary inscription photographs were inspected.

The extension from garment to ‘constant/custom/frequent’ cannot be reconstructed as a fully dated semantic chain from the inspected sources. Shuowen/Duan report extension; bronze attestations support early non-garment use, but do not identify when or by what precise semantic pathway it developed.

No independent direct evidence was found for a whole-graph phonetic loan of the garment graph to a separate spoken word. The sources instead support 常 as a phonetic compound with 尚 as sound component; do not conflate that role with whole-graph borrowing.
No claim about corruption or scribal error is supported. The reported historical mixing of 常 and 嘗 concerns graphic usage and is not evidence that 常 itself arose through corruption.

No specific date is established for the cited bronze, bamboo-slip, or received textual attestations on the inspected pages; dates should not be supplied without checking catalogued artifacts or manuscript editions.

No inspected source established a Shang oracle-bone form for 常. The consulted databases report bronze, Warring States, Chu manuscript, small-seal, or received Shuowen material, but available page text did not establish a first attestation date.

The clothing sense is reported in named bronze and Warring States examples, but the inspected references do not date those artifacts or establish which is earliest. No primary inscription image was inspected.

The garment-to-‘constant/custom/frequent’ semantic path is not fully dated. Sources assert phonetic borrowing or extension; the reported bronze custom/law use shows early non-garment usage but does not itself explain the semantic transition.

CUHK reports a competing view attributed to 朱駿聲 that 常 originally meant a flag and 裳 the garment. CUHK argues bronze clothing examples weigh against it; the primary inscription images were not inspected, so the dispute is recorded rather than independently adjudicated.
CUHK reports ancient mixing of 常 and 嘗 that diminished after the Ming and Qing; the consulted source does not establish that 常 itself arose by corruption. No specific corruption claim is supported.
No direct evidence located for a whole-graph loan of garment 常 to an unrelated spoken word. Evidence supports a phonetic-compound analysis with 尚 as sound component; these are distinct claims.

The identification of 巾 as the clothing-related semantic element and 尚 as phonetic is supported by the inspected specialist sources. 尚's own earliest depicted referent has competing interpretations and is not resolved here; this uncertainty does not negate its independently supported later phonetic role.

No 常-specific reusable bronze or Chu manuscript image was established from the searches. Direct candidate URLs failed or led to category pages; the sole proposed glyph is a modern seal-script vector redraw with explicit public-domain provenance.
The Commons page provides source references for the seal drawing but the linked underlying glyph image itself could not be opened through the browser tool. No pixel-level inspection is claimed.
The source page provides a corrected direct target for 常-seal.svg, but the browser could not fetch the SVG itself; harness acquisition may still fail despite the page's valid file link.

常-bronze.svg appeared in a Commons category listing, but opening its file page failed with a cache miss. Its specific script period, source references, and reuse rights remain unverified, so it is not proposed.

Opened alternate-version links for oracle, bronze, and Chu-slip script led to broad categories and did not establish additional 常-specific images. No artifact photographs or visual inspection are claimed.
